rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology Sec. 2.1 and Results Sec. 3 - the study uses its own hydrant flowmeter telemetry records (627 hydrants, 2015 season, 228,855 daily observations) and climatic station data from Sector II of Canal del Zujar Irrigation District to train and test decision trees optimised by NSGA-II; Tables 3-4 report its own classification results.
rows.notes: The study's own result is the predictive accuracy of optimal decision trees in forecasting whether a farmer irrigates on a given day (Table 4: 68-100% of positive events, 93-100% of negative events correctly classified on the test set). It does not measure or model any reduction in water loss, water use or energy use resulting from applying the model; the Conclusions only assert that knowing event occurrence one day ahead 'might' allow pumping optimisation and energy cost reduction. The claimed effect (minimising water and energy loss) is therefore a hypothesised downstream benefit of a precondition (event prediction) that the study establishes, so Q2 is 'no' and upstream is set. Note also that the model forecasts farmer behaviour for district managers rather than advising farmers when to irrigate, so it is only loosely an 'app_scheduling' technology; and the review's context sentence misdescribes it as predicting irrigation amount (that is the authors' 2018 paper). The study does state a limitation of its own prediction result (class imbalance, CT2/CT3 learn negative events better) and reports no dispersion measure, but as Q2 is 'no' these are recorded as 'no'.

notes: Full text appears complete (post-print, Computers and Electronics in Agriculture 157:173-180). Figures 4a-c (tree schemes) are not rendered in the text but do not affect the rating. The study is a single-district, single-season (2015) modelling exercise with validation against observed hydrant operation records.
